query: For refractory high-entropy alloys intended for jet-turbine applications, what single intervention could improve high-temperature mechanical capability while limiting density and preserving room-temperature performance? Formulate one hypothesis that specifies the intervention, its mechanism, the expected improvement relative to a relevant baseline, the temperature and loading conditions under which it should hold, supporting evidence from prior studies, and a decisive experiment with a result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Introducing a trace amount of boron (≈0.2 at%) into a lightweight, Al-modified refractory high‐entropy alloy (e.g., TaNbVTiAl0.2) will strengthen grain boundaries via the formation of ultrathin boride films. This, in turn, will improve high‐temperature yield strength and creep resistance under jet‐turbine conditions while preserving room‐temperature ductility and maintaining low alloy density.
generation.material_initial_state: A lightweight refractory high‐entropy alloy with a single BCC matrix modified by aluminum (e.g., TaNbVTiAl0.2) that already exhibits a good balance of room-temperature strength, ductility, and reduced density.
generation.intervention: Add a trace amount (around 0.2 at%) of boron into the melt during alloy fabrication to promote its segregation to grain boundaries and the formation of nanoscale boride phases.
generation.conditions: The alloy will be evaluated under tensile and compressive loading at room temperature and at high temperatures up to approximately 1200°C, with additional consideration for cyclic thermal fatigue conditions representative of jet-turbine environments.
generation.structural_mediator: Grain boundaries that incorporate an ultrathin, well-dispersed boride phase along with a stabilized BCC matrix.
generation.mechanism: Trace boron is expected to segregate to grain boundaries during solidification and subsequent heat treatments, forming nano-scale boride layers that impede grain-boundary sliding and dislocation motion at elevated temperatures. This grain boundary strengthening mechanism enhances high-temperature yield strength and creep resistance, while the very low boron content minimizes any adverse effects on the room-temperature microstructure and overall density.
generation.predicted_outcome: At high temperatures (e.g., near 1200°C), the alloy should demonstrate an elevated yield strength improvement on the order of roughly 10–20% versus the undoped baseline, along with reduced creep rates, while maintaining similar room-temperature ductility and negligible (<5%) changes in density.
generation.baseline: The performance of the undoped TaNbVTiAl0.2 alloy as previously reported (e.g., by studies on lightweight RHEAs modified with Al for density reduction and strength improvement).
generation.boundary: The improvement is anticipated in the high-temperature regime pertinent to jet-turbine applications; however, the beneficial effect may be sensitive to the exact boron content, processing conditions, and the long-term thermal stability of the boride films.
generation.uncertainty: Uncertainties include the long-term stability of the ultrathin boride phases under prolonged high-temperature exposure and cyclic loading, and whether the beneficial segregation observed in MoNbTaW (PMC9586648) extends in a similar manner to an Al-modified alloy (PMC7516739, PMC8746096). The synthesis combining trace boron doping with an Al-induced lightening strategy is novel and untested in this specific system.

falsification_experiment.design: Fabricate two sets of alloys with identical processing: one set of the baseline TaNbVTiAl0.2 alloy and one set doped with approximately 0.2 at% boron. After homogenization and proper thermal treatment, perform systematic mechanical tests at room temperature and at high temperatures up to 1200°C, including creep experiments. Complement mechanical testing with microstructural evaluations (using TEM and atom probe tomography) to confirm boron segregation and the presence of nano-scale boride films at grain boundaries.
measurements: High-temperature yield strength and creep rate at ~1200°C
Grain boundary chemical analysis via TEM/APT
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: The hypothesis will be falsified if the boron-doped alloy does not achieve at least a 10% improvement in high-temperature yield strength (or a corresponding reduction in creep rate) compared to the undoped baseline, or if room-temperature performance degrades significantly (e.g., >15% reduction in ductility) or if density increases by more than 5%.

cited_evidence.text: Xu et al. [] reduced the density of the Ti50-xAlxV20Nb20Mo10 RHEA from 6.102 g/cm3 (Ti40Al10V20Nb20Mo10) to 5.876 g/cm3 (Ti30Al20V20Nb20Mo10) by adjusting the Al content, and the room-temperature specific yield strength increased from 147.49 MPa*cm3/g to 202.01 MPa*cm3/g. Although the density and specific strength of these alloys are significantly improved after the addition of aluminum, their plasticity is generally reduced. Therefore, choosing a refractory high-entropy alloy with both high strength and high plasticity as a matrix, and then reducing its density by adding light elements such as Al, is an effective method to obtain structural materials with high strength, low density, and good plasticity. The recently reported TaNbVTi alloy meets the requirements of the matrix very well []. Furthermore, Yang et al. [] reported that the arc-melted NbTiVTaAl0.25 HEA has a low density of 8.78 g/cm3 and reasonable plasticity greater than 50%. Nevertheless, the yield strength of this alloy is only 1330 MPa (specific strength of 151.48 MPa*cm3/g), which has the possibility of further improvement compared with most refractory high-entropy alloys.

AbstractA series of novel lightweight TaNbVTi-based refractory high entropy alloys (RHEA) were fabricated through ball-milling and spark plasma sintering (SPS). The reinforced phase of TiO precipitates were in-situ formed due to the introduction of Al2O3 ceramic particles. The RHEA with 15% Al2O3 exhibits a high compressive yield strength (1837 MPa) and a low density (7.75 g/cm3) with an adequate ductility retention. The yield strength and density are 32% higher and 15% lower, respectively, compared to the RHEA without Al2O3 addition. The specific yield strength (237 MPa cm3/g) of the RHEAs is much higher than that of other reported RHEAs, and is mainly ascribed to the introduction of high volume fraction of Al2O3 additives, resulting in solid solution strengthening and precipitation strengthening. Meanwhile, the ductile matrix is responsible for the good compressive plasticity.Keywords: refractory high entropy alloy, microstructure, powder metallurgy, sintering, mechanical property

After the first development of RHEAs in 2010, over 150 kinds of compositions have been reported, with their potential for use in high-temperature applications such as gas turbine engines and rocket nozzles. Various studies focused on ductility enhancement [,], better oxidation resistance [], and nuclear reactor material applications [,]. According to a review by Senkov et al. [], the only alloys to pass high-temperature compression tests at 1600°C were MoNbTaW and MoNbTaVW. The main reason for the difficulty to perform compression tests at extremely high temperatures is the lack of suitable material as a jig material that provides high strength at extremely high temperatures. Recently, Wang et al. strengthened the grain boundary of an MoNbTaW-refractory high-entropy alloy through doping with B or C in trace amount, which simultaneously increases room-temperature strength and toughness []. This study provides a good strategy to increase the ductility of RHEAs by doping suitable elements.
